text: A catalog with perfect metadata that nobody can actually find is worthless — the same publish failure mode from the metadata lifecycle, specific to catalogs. The entire value collapses into one question: when someone searches, do they find the right answer quickly?

Four capabilities separate a useful catalog from a glorified spreadsheet. Full-text search across both business and technical metadata. Faceted filtering by owner, system, status, or sensitivity. Relationship navigation between glossary and dictionary. And usage-based ranking, surfacing what's actually queried above what nobody touches.

A general web search mostly works on relevance alone, because the web doesn't have a reliable owner or status field to filter on. A data catalog does — because Chapters 2 through 4 spent enormous effort getting those fields documented consistently. Faceted search is where that upfront investment actually pays off.

A new analyst searches 'customer revenue.' A good result set surfaces the Net Revenue glossary term first, then OrderTotal — which implements it and is heavily used — then a related Customer Lifetime Value term. A poorly built catalog just returns every table with 'customer' in its name, unsorted.
Next lesson: cataloging business and technical metadata — how the two actually get combined in practice.
